title: Eighty years in robes
hook: the elder Bakkula, eighty years a monk and never ill

segments.voice: Yesterday: acchariya, the Buddha's own marvel, and your line, catch it as it begins.

An old friend turns up after a lifetime apart, and the first thing out of his mouth is a question nobody else would dare ask. That's how the hundred and twenty-fourth discourse begins. The elder Bakkula is staying near Rajagaha. A naked ascetic named Kassapa, a friend from Bakkula's lay days, comes to see him. How long have you been a monk, friend Bakkula? Eighty years. Then Kassapa asks a blunt personal question about desire, and Bakkula doesn't answer it the way it's asked.
screen: `AN OLD FRIEND, A LIFETIME LATER.` → `HOW LONG A MONK? EIGHTY YEARS.` → `A BLUNT QUESTION.`

segments.voice: You shouldn't ask it that way, Bakkula says. Ask instead: in eighty years, how many times has a thought of sensual desire even come up? And he answers that one: not once. Then a long list follows, almost an inventory of a life. In eighty years he never accepted a robe from a householder; he wore cast-off cloth. He never sat down to an invitation meal. He never leaned against a wall to rest, never lay down on a bed. He never had an illness, not even for as long as it takes to pull a cow's teat, and never took so much as a piece of medicinal fruit. On the eighth day after he went forth, he says, he was freed. Each item ends with the same refrain from the reciters: this too we remember as a wonderful quality of the venerable Bakkula. Kassapa is so moved he asks to go forth under him, and in time reaches the goal himself. Then the ending. One day Bakkula takes a key and goes from dwelling to dwelling: come out, venerables; today I'll pass away. And he does, sitting among the monks. The Buddha never appears in this discourse. Bakkula's way was unusually strict, and plenty of Buddhists, then and now, take medicine, sit at invitations and wear donated robes. What rings true across eighty years is simpler: a body used carefully, a life kept plain, and a death met sitting up, among friends.
screen: `ASK IT ANOTHER WAY` · `A PLAIN, EIGHTY-YEAR INVENTORY` · `NEVER ILL, NOT EVEN A MOMENT` · `A KEY, AND A QUIET DEATH` · then, large: `EIGHTY YEARS IN ROBES.`

segments.voice: Bodies differ, and this isn't about comparing with Bakkula's health. Move your attention slowly through the body, and wherever something is working, a hand that holds, lungs that fill, eyes that read, give it a silent thank you. Where something hurts, just acknowledge it carried you here too.
Bakkula. The elder who spent eighty years a monk, never ill even for a moment, and met his death sitting among the monks.
Your line: a life kept plain. Care for a body can be simple. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Theravada tradition Bakkula is remembered as the monk foremost in good health, and the rag-robe and solitary practices he kept are among the optional ascetic practices (dhutanga) some forest monks still take up today.

chat.says: Do Buddhists have to refuse medicine and never lie down, like Bakkula?
options: No: his way was unusually strict; many Buddhists take medicine and accept robes.
Yes: every monk is expected to live exactly as Bakkula did, for life.
Yes: the Buddha himself ordered all monks to follow Bakkula's rules.
